title: Primer · Accounting Concepts in ERPNext
subtitle: The ten accounting ideas a functional consultant must be able to explain at a whiteboard, and the ERPNext screen each one lives on
outcomes: Explain double entry and the accounting equation without notes
Place every account type in the right report and recognise a normal balance
Describe the three ledgers in ERPNext and what question each one answers
Know when a situation needs a Journal Entry and when it needs a business document
Run four checks that prove a client's books agree before you trust any report

slides.title: Every number has two sides, and ERPNext refuses to pretend otherwise
bullets: Accounting records the effect of a transaction twice: something received, something given
Assets equal liabilities plus equity, and every posting preserves that balance
ERPNext will not save an unbalanced Journal Entry, which is a teaching tool as much as a control
Ledger rows are created by vouchers and cannot be edited afterwards, only reversed
Once a client understands this, every report stops looking like magic

rows: Each posting has an equal debit and credit
A document that creates ledger rows on submit
Posted rows are read-only; corrections are new documents
Unbalanced entries are refused by the system

slides.notes: Open the course with the whiteboard, not the screen. Draw the equation, then show that a sale increases an asset and increases income, which sits in equity. A consultant who cannot explain this in five minutes will lose the room to the client's accountant within a week. The ERPNext detail, that unbalanced vouchers are refused, gives the concept teeth.

callout.title: Ask for two sides, always
callout.text: When a client describes a transaction, respond with 'what is the other side?'. It is the fastest way to expose a process that has never been thought through.

slides.title: Five types, two normal balances, three reports
bullets: Asset and expense accounts normally carry debit balances; liability, equity and income carry credits
Account type drives which report an account appears in, not the account's name
Group accounts organise the tree; only leaf accounts accept postings
A wrongly typed account is the single most common reason a balance sheet looks strange
Chart design is a client decision, but type selection is a consultant responsibility
slides.notes: Show a P&L and a balance sheet side by side, then click one account and show its type. The link between type and report is what most users miss. Malaysian SMEs often arrive with a chart produced by an accountant in Excel; your job is to map each row to a type, not to redesign the chart to your own taste.
paths: Accounts → Chart of Accounts → Account → Account Type

slides.title: Accrual accounting, and why tax is a liability not a cost
bullets: Accrual recognises income when earned and expenses when incurred, not when cash moves
Cash accounting recognises the same events when money changes hands, which suits tiny businesses
Under accrual, a sale creates a receivable immediately and the cash arrives later
SST collected is never revenue: it is a liability owed to LHDN until remitted
Mixing the two bases inside one company produces reports that cannot be reconciled
slides.notes: This is where clients argue, because their previous system may have been cash-based. ERPNext is accrual by default, and pretending otherwise creates an unworkable receivables ledger. Explain tax as a pass-through early, or someone will report SST as revenue and the gross margin will be wrong by ten per cent forever.

callout.title: SST is collected, not earned
callout.text: SST Payable is a liability cleared when you file and pay. It never touches the profit and loss account.

slides.title: One transaction, three different books
bullets: The general ledger answers what the business is worth and what it earned
The stock ledger answers where the goods are and what they cost
The payment ledger answers who owes whom, invoice by invoice
Each ledger is fed by different documents, which is why one mistake is invisible in the other two
A consultant reconciles all three at month end, not just the trial balance

rows: What did we earn, own and owe?
Where is the stock and what is it worth?
Who owes what, document by document?
Do all three agree, line by line?

slides.notes: Draw three columns and put a sales invoice at the top of one, a delivery note at the top of the second, and the payment at the top of the third. This picture explains ninety per cent of month-end confusion, including why a fully paid invoice can still leave a stock problem and why a stock discrepancy does not always move profit in the period the client expects.

callout.title: One mistake, two ledgers
callout.text: Receiving goods without a purchase receipt moves stock in reality and nothing in ERPNext, so both stock and profit are wrong until it is posted.

slides.title: Control accounts and party ledgers
bullets: The receivable control account holds the total owed by all customers
Each customer also has a ledger, and the sum of those ledgers must equal the control account
ERPNext keeps both in one system, so the control account is derived rather than typed
An unreconciled payment breaks the equality between party ledgers and the control account
Never post a manual journal to a control account to make a report balance

rows: Party ledgers equal the control account

slides.notes: Consultants see this defect constantly: a journal entry posted to Debtors to fix a small difference, which hides an unallocated receipt and breaks every ageing report. Say plainly that a control account is a check, not a bucket. The correct fix is to allocate the payment or write off with an approved document.

callout.title: Never journal into Debtors
callout.text: A manual entry to a control account breaks the link to party ledgers. Fix the allocation or post a proper credit note.

slides.title: Follow one sale from document to trial balance
bullets: Use the sample company's invoice: 1,200.00 net, 120.00 SST, 1,320.00 total
Do this on the learner's own site so the numbers are real, not a slide
The point is to see the same transaction appear in four different reports
Note which report shows tax separately and which shows only the receivable
If any step is empty, a document was saved as a draft instead of submitted
slides.notes: This is the moment theory becomes a habit. Ask the learner to predict what the P&L will show before opening it: they should say income 1,200 and no tax, because tax is a liability. If they say 1,320, revisit the accrual slide. Doing this on their own site, rather than reading a screenshot, is what makes it stick.

slides.title: Four checks that prove the books agree
bullets: A trial balance that does not balance means a posting went somewhere impossible
Debtors in the general ledger must equal the total of customer balances
The stock account balance must equal the value in the stock ledger
Bank in the ledger must equal the bank statement once reconciled
These four checks take ten minutes and prevent a month of argument

rows: Balance Sheet vs Stock Balance value

slides.notes: Give the learner a routine they can run in front of a client. The stock check is the one that surprises people, because a wrong valuation or a missing repost shows up here and nowhere else. If the stock ledger and the stock account disagree, stop and fix that before closing the period.

callout.title: Ten minutes, every month
callout.text: Run these four checks before any management report leaves your desk. It is cheaper than defending a wrong number.

slides.title: When a journal is right, and when it is a workaround
bullets: A Journal Entry is for adjustments with no business document: accruals, depreciation, corrections
A purchase invoice is not a journal: it carries supplier, tax and payment terms
A customer invoice is not a journal: it carries stock, revenue and receivables together
Journals should be few, named consistently and traceable to a reason
A client with hundreds of journals per month has a process problem, not an accounting one
slides.notes: Consultants inherit journals the previous team used to patch around missing documents. Ask to see a month of them and classify each: adjustment, or workaround. The second category is your implementation backlog. Reversal dates are worth demonstrating because they let a client accrue at month end without editing the entry later.

slides.title: The four adjustments every close needs
bullets: Accruals match costs to the period they belong to, usually with an automatic reversal
Prepayments spread a payment over the periods it covers
Depreciation allocates an asset's cost over its useful life, never in one hit
A period closing voucher freezes history so back-dated entries cannot rewrite a closed month
Closing is a sequence with owners and dates, not a Friday afternoon

rows: Journal Entry per period, or deferred expense
Trial Balance and stock value check

slides.notes: Do not teach closing as a button. Teach it as an order of operations with a checklist and a named owner, then show the documents. If the client has never closed a period, run the first close with them, because that is where the process either becomes real or collapses into a spreadsheet.

callout.title: Close, then report
callout.text: Reports generated before the close are drafts. Say so, or the client will quote a number that changes twice.

slides.title: Five questions before you trust a client's trial balance
bullets: Are there unallocated payments, which make receivables overstate what is owed?
Does the stock account equal the stock ledger value, to the sen?
Are there draft invoices that the business believes are issued?
Is every control account reconciled to its party ledgers?
Has the period been closed, or can last month still change?

rows: Sales Invoice and Purchase Invoice lists

slides.notes: End the primer with the questions a client will one day ask you, phrased so that you can answer them from a report rather than an opinion. A consultant who can run these five checks in fifteen minutes is worth more than one who can configure forty features, because trust is built on numbers that survive scrutiny.

callout.title: Drafts are not invoices
callout.text: A saved-but-unsubmitted invoice posts nothing. Clients routinely believe they have billed a customer who has never been invoiced.

lab.title: Lab · Trace money through the books and break the balance
steps: Post a Journal Entry: debit Petty Cash 500.00, credit Bank 500.00, cost centre Main
Open the General Ledger and confirm both lines appear with the same voucher number
Run the Trial Balance and confirm debits equal credits and Petty Cash reads 500.00
Deliberately remove the credit line and try to save, recording the exact message ERPNext returns
Restore the credit, post an accrual of 300.00 to Electricity with a reversal date of the first of next month
Confirm the reversal entry is created automatically on the reversal date
Post a Sales Invoice for 1,200.00 plus 120.00 SST and follow it through the P&L and Balance Sheet
Run the four checks from Concept 7 and write down the result of each
lab.done: The unbalanced entry was refused, the accrual reversed itself, the invoice appears as 1,200.00 income and 120.00 liability, and all four reconciliation checks have a written result.

quiz.question: Which statement about double entry in ERPNext is true?
options: ERPNext allows unbalanced journals but warns
ERPNext refuses to save an unbalanced journal entry
Only sales documents are double entry
Double entry applies to stock but not to accounts
quiz.why: Every posting needs equal debits and credits. ERPNext blocks the save, which makes the accounting equation a system rule rather than advice.

quiz.question: Which account carries a normal credit balance?
quiz.why: Income accounts such as Sales increase on the credit side. Assets and expenses increase on the debit side.

quiz.question: Which ledger answers the question 'who owes us, invoice by invoice'?
quiz.why: The payment ledger tracks outstanding amounts per document and is cleared only when payments are allocated to invoices.

quiz.question: A client's debtors balance is out by 1,320.00. What is the correct first move?
options: Post a journal entry to Debtors for the difference
Check for an unallocated customer payment
quiz.why: A difference in a control account is almost always an allocation problem. Journaling into the control account hides the cause and breaks the party ledger link.

quiz.question: SST collected on an invoice should appear where?
options: As a liability on the balance sheet
quiz.why: Tax collected is held for LHDN until remitted. Treating it as income overstates revenue by the tax rate.

narration: Before the walkthroughs, the concepts, because a consultant who cannot explain the books will lose the client's accountant in the first meeting. Accounting runs on one equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity, and every transaction touches it twice. ERPNext enforces that twice-ness by refusing to save an unbalanced journal entry, which makes the rule visible. There are five account types, and the type decides the report: assets, liabilities and equity on the balance sheet, income and expenses on the profit and loss. Malaysian clients often arrive with a chart built in a spreadsheet, so your job is to map each row to a type, not to impose your own taste. Next, accrual accounting: income when earned, expenses when incurred. Tax collected is never income; it is a liability cleared when you file. Then the three ledgers. The general ledger says what the business earned and owns. The stock ledger says where the goods are and what they cost. The payment ledger says who owes what, document by document. One mistake is often invisible in two of the three, which is why month end reconciles all of them. Control accounts and party ledgers must agree, and you never fix a difference by journaling into debtors. Finally, journals: right for accruals and depreciation, wrong as a replacement for a purchase invoice or a sale. Close with four checks and five questions, because trust is built on numbers that survive scrutiny.
